201.1AC Power Systems Inspection and MaintenanceCourse Title:201.1 AC Power Systems Inspection and Maintenance - Part 1: AC Power Systems Theory
Part 1AC Power Systems TheoryCourse Structure:Introduction
Module 1: Review of AC Theory
• Examine the theory and principles of alternating current power systems
Course Duration:1 Hour0 Minutes1
Replaced
Course Description:This course reviews and deepens the REW's understanding of alternating current (AC) power system theory relevant to railway infrastructure. This learning session examines core principles (sinusoidal waveforms, phasors, RMS values, frequency, impedance, power factor, real/reactive/apparent power, single‑phase and three‑phase systems, transformers, and basic fault/current flow behavior), and supplies practical examples tied to traction AC networks. Emphasis is on applying theory to common inspection and maintenance tasks, interpreting measurements, and diagnosing typical AC-related issues encountered on site. The course combines classroom theory, worked examples, and application exercises to prepare REWs for subsequent hands‑on inspection and maintenance modules.
Course Outcomes:Technicians will be able to explain core AC concepts (sinusoidal waveforms, phasors, RMS, frequency, impedance, power factor, and real/reactive/apparent power), distinguish single‑phase and three‑phase behaviors, and describe transformer and basic fault/current flow characteristics. They will also be expected to perform basic calculations, and interpret measurements taken on traction AC networks. REWs will also show how to apply theoretical knowledge to identify and diagnose common AC-related issues during inspections and maintenance; while confidently translating classroom learning into practical tasks, preparing them for the hands‑on inspection and maintenance modules that follow.
Learning Objectives:• Explain sinusoidal waveforms, phasors, RMS values and frequency in the context of AC power systems. • Define impedance and apply it to simple circuit examples. • Explain power factor and differentiate real, reactive and apparent power. • Distinguish electrical behavior and loading characteristics of single‑phase vs three‑phase systems. • Describe transformer function, basic configuration types, and how they affect voltage/current in traction networks. • Describe basic fault types and typical current flow patterns during faults. • Perform basic AC calculations (RMS, apparent/real/reactive power, impedance magnitude) for typical inspection scenarios. • Interpret measurement readings (voltage, current, phase relationships, power factor) from site instruments and diagrams. • Identify common AC-related faults and failure indicators during inspections (unbalanced phases, abnormal voltages/currents, poor power factor). • Diagnose likely causes of measured anomalies and recommend appropriate immediate actions or escalation. • Translate theoretical results into practical inspection and maintenance steps and prepare for hands‑on follow‑up tasks.

201.1Basic Electrical Theory – Part 1: Fundamentals Course Title:201.1 Basic Electrical Theory – Part 1: Fundamentals
Course Structure:Module 1: Fundamentals
• AC/DC Theory
• Ohm's Law
• Power Calculations
• Three-Phase Systems
Module 2 Grounding Systems
• Fundamentals of Distribution System Grounding
• Direct Current (DC) Traction Power System Grounding
• Overhead Contact System (OCS) Grounding
Module 3: Short Circuit Theory - Overview
• Methods of Bond Attachment (cad weld, spot weld, arc weld, mechanical, structure)
• Symmetrical Components
Course Duration:1 Hour0 Minutes1
Course Description:This course introduces technicians and entry-level engineers to core electrical principles and practical power-system concepts needed for safe design, operation, and troubleshooting. The course covers AC and DC theory, Ohm’s Law, power and basic circuit calculations, and three‑phase system behavior, then examines grounding practices for distribution systems, DC traction and overhead contact systems, and the fundamentals of short‑circuit theory including symmetrical components and common methods of bond attachment (cad weld, spot/arc weld, mechanical). Emphasis is placed on real‑world examples, calculations, and best practices to build a solid foundation for further study and field application.
Learning Objectives:• Identify basic differences between AC and DC and read simple circuit diagrams to predict whether voltages and currents are steady or alternating. • Use V = I·R to solve for voltage, current, or resistance in basic circuits and check whether meter readings make sense. • Calculate simple power (P = V·I) and recognize the difference between real and apparent power for common loads. • Convert simple line/phase values and explain what happens when one phase is heavier or lighter than the others. • Explain the purpose of grounding, identify grounding conductors, and recognize basic touch/step hazard concerns. • Describe grounding goals for DC traction systems, spot likely fault paths, and suggest basic steps to reduce stray current. • Explain an OCS layout and find grounding points and state why correct grounding keeps equipment and people safe. • Recognize common bond methods (cad weld, spot/arc weld, mechanical) and choose an appropriate method for a simple field connection. • Describe in plain terms that unbalanced systems can be split into simpler sequence parts and use that idea to understand basic fault effects.

201.1Basic Electrical Theory – Part 2: ControlsCourse Title:Basic Electrical Theory – Part 2: Controls
Course Structure:Module 1: Fundamentals
• Relay Logic
• Interlocks
• Programmable Logical Controller (PLC) and Input / Output (I/O’s)
Course Duration:1 Hour0 Minutes1
Course Description:This course introduces technicians to the basics of control systems used in industrial and traction settings, covering relay logic, interlocks, and basic PLC inputs/outputs. Students will learn to read simple ladder diagrams, identify common relay and interlock layouts, and see how PLC I/O connects to sensors and actuators. The course stresses hands‑on troubleshooting, safe work practices, and basic fault diagnosis so participants can spot control problems, make simple repairs, and clearly report issues to maintenance or engineers.
Learning Objectives:• Identify common relay components on a ladder diagram and explain how coil and contact interactions control circuit operation. • Trace a simple relay circuit to diagnose and correct a fault (stuck contact, blown fuse, or open coil) using basic tests and safe procedures. • Describe the purpose of mechanical and electrical interlocks and identify interlock locations in a typical control panel or machine. • Given an interlock failure scenario, determine the likely cause and outline the correct sequence of checks and corrective actions to restore safe operation. • Recognize basic PLC hardware (CPU, input modules, output modules) and map simple field devices (limit switch, motor starter) to PLC I/O points. • Read a simple ladder logic rung to predict PLC behavior for given input conditions and use basic troubleshooting steps to verify I/O faults.

201.2Substation Equipment – Part 1: Switchgear FundamentalsCourse Title:201.2 Substation Equipment – Part 1: Switchgear Fundamentals
Course Structure:Module 1: Switchgear
• Power Transformers
• Instrument transformers (CTs/PTs)
• Vacuum Circuit breakers
• Disconnect switches
• Meters
• Ground switches
• Ground mat
• Bus configurations
• Rectifier
Course Duration:4 Hours0 Minutes4
In-Class Duration:2 Hours0 Minutes2
Workshop Duration:2 Hours0 Minutes2
Course Description:In this course, Rail Electrical Workers receive a clear, practical introduction to the key switchgear and support equipment used in substations. Through focused lessons and real‑world examples, participants will learn to identify and explain the functions of power transformers, CTs/PTs, vacuum circuit breakers, disconnect and ground switches, meters, ground mats, bus configurations, and rectifiers, understand how these components interact to control and protect power, and apply basic safety and inspection practices. By the end of the course learners will be able to recognize common equipment, interpret simple layouts, spot obvious faults or unsafe conditions, and communicate findings effectively to maintenance or engineering teams.
In-Class Learning Objectives:
• Identify the main parts of a power transformer and explain its role in voltage step‑up/step‑down and basic safety checks before work. • Describe the purpose of CTs and PTs, read their primary/secondary ratings, and explain why correct polarity and burden matter for metering/protection. • Identify a vacuum circuit breaker, explain its operation principle and trip function, and list common signs of malfunction. • Locate and describe the function of disconnect switches, and demonstrate correct isolation sequence procedures for visual inspection. • Identify common substation meters (voltage, current, energy), read basic meter displays, and report abnormal readings to maintenance. • Explain the purpose of ground switches, identify their positions, and describe safe procedures for applying and verifying grounding. • Describe what a ground mat is, its role in personnel safety and fault dissipation, and identify visible signs of damage or degradation. • Compare common bus arrangements (single‑bus, breaker‑and‑half, ring bus) and explain how configuration affects reliability and switching operations. • Identify a rectifier in the substation, explain its function converting AC to DC, and state typical maintenance strategy, along with the potential fault indicators that may appear outside of scheduled maintenance.
Workshop Activities:Focus: Switchgear
• Welcome, objectives, safety brief • Mini-lecture: transformer components, safety checks, quick Q&A. • Hands-on/nameplate exercise: CT/PT ratings, polarity/burden examples. • Visual ID: vacuum breaker and disconnects — trainer-led demo of common fault signs.
• Isolation sequence simulation: group walkthrough using checklist and role-play.
• Meter-reading exercise: interpret displays, log an abnormal reading, complete short report.
• Bus arrangement diagram exercise and short discussion of reliability/switching.
• Quick summary, takeaways, and next steps/resources.

201.2Substation Equipment – Part 2: Protection SystemsCourse Title:201.2 Substation Equipment – Part 2: Protection Systems
Course Note: Testing is not covered at this level. This will come later in the curriculum.
Course Structure:Module 1: AC Protective Relays
• Functions
• Time curves
• Display Navigation – Trips and Alarms
Module 2: DC Protective Relays
• Functions
• Overcurrent and Ground Structure
• Display Navigation – Trips and Alarms
Module 3: DC Rail-to-Ground System (R2G)
• Functions
• Purpose
Course Duration:8 Hours0 Minutes8
In-Class Duration:5 Hours0 Minutes5
Workshop Duration:3 Hours0 Minutes3
Course Description:This course introduces Rail Electrical Workers to the basic role and operation of protection equipment used in substations and DC traction systems, without covering testing procedures. Learners will understand the functions and common time‑curves of AC protective relays, how to navigate relay displays for trips and alarms, the purpose and basic structure of DC protective relays including overcurrent and ground protection, and the role and intent of the DC rail‑to‑ground (R2G) system. The course emphasizes clear, practical explanations and simple examples so participants can recognize protection devices, interpret basic relay indications, and communicate protection events or concerns to maintenance and traction power control.
In-Class Learning Objectives:
• Describe the basic functions of AC protective relays and explain common time‑curve types (instantaneous, inverse, definite‑time). • Read a relay display to identify trips and alarms and explain the meaning of basic status and event indicators. • Explain the purpose and main components of DC protective relays, including overcurrent and ground protection roles. • Identify typical relay indications for overcurrent and ground faults and describe the immediate actions to report or escalate. • Describe the purpose and operation of the DC rail‑to‑ground (R2G) system and how it supports traction system safety. • Recognize common protection devices in a substation or traction panel (relays, CTs, trip units) and state their primary functions. • Interpret simple protection events (e.g., trip cause, affected circuit) from provided relay information and summarize findings for maintenance. • Communicate protection concerns clearly to maintenance and traction power control, including equipment ID, observed indications, and recommended next steps.
Workshop Activities:Focus: Protection Systems
• Welcome, objectives, safety brief, and pre-check knowledge poll.
• Mini-lecture: AC relay basics and time-curve types with one-line examples.
• Demo: Relay display walkthrough — trips, alarms, status lights, event log structure.
• Hands-on (or simulated) exercise 1: Read 2 relay screenshots/logs and identify trip/alarms
• Mini-lecture: DC relay components and R2G operation with schematic overview.
• Group activity: Identify protection devices in a substation panel photo and state primary functions.
• Scenario exercise: Interpret a provided protection event (trip cause, affected circuit) from relay data; prepare a one-paragraph maintenance summary.
• Reporting practice: Role-play briefings — communicate incident to maintenance/traction control using a standard form.
• Wrap-up, takeaways, and recommended next steps/resources.

201.2Substation Equipment – Part 3: Auxiliary ComponentsCourse Title:201.2 Substation Equipment – Part 3: Auxiliary Components
Course Note: This course is an overview to supply descriptions, explanations of purpose, and images.
Course Structure:Module 1: Auxiliary Components
• LCMS Panel DCAM Panel
• DCAM Panel (Min. Voltage Switchgear
• Battery Chargers
• DC Control Voltage
• Batteries
• HVAC
• Network Equipment
• UPS
• Emergency Trip
• Fire Alarm Panel
• Fire Extinguishers
• Eye Wash
Course Duration:4 Hours0 Minutes4
In-Class Duration:3 Hours0 Minutes3
Workshop Duration:1 Hours0 Minutes1
Course Description:This course offers Rail Electrical Workers a clear overview of the auxiliary systems that support substation and traction power equipment. The learner will be provide with descriptions of common components, including LCMS panels, DCAM panels, battery chargers and batteries, DC control voltage systems, UPS, rectifiers, HVAC, network equipment, emergency trip and fire alarm panels, fire extinguishers, eye wash stations, and other safety gear. Each component's purpose will be explained, along with basic operation and where it fits into overall substation reliability and safety. The learning content emphasizes plain‑language explanations, practical photographs and diagrams to aid recognition, and simple guidance on what visible signs to report or escalate. By the end, learners will be able to identify auxiliary components, state their functions, and communicate observed issues to maintenance or traction power control.
In-Class Learning Objectives:
• Identify LCMS panel elements and explain how alarms and status indicators communicate substation conditions to power control. • Identify DCAM panel elements and explain how alarms and status indicators communicate substation conditions to power control. • Describe the purpose of battery chargers in maintaining DC control voltage and recognize common visible indicators of charger failure. • Explain the role of DC control voltage in operating protection and control devices and identify where DC systems interface with equipment. • Identify battery types used in substations, state their role in backup power, and recognize obvious signs (leaks, swelling, corrosion) that should be reported. • Describe why HVAC is used in substations (temperature/humidity control for equipment reliability) and note environmental conditions that warrant escalation. • Explain the purpose of network equipment (communications, telemetry, remote monitoring) and identify basic indicators of communication loss. • Describe a UPS’s role in providing short‑term power support to critical control and monitoring systems and recognize front‑panel alarms or status lights to report. • Explain the function and purpose of emergency trip systems and how an activated emergency trip is indicated and should be reported. • Identify the fire alarm panel and its basic indicators, and explain the required immediate actions when a fire alarm condition is observed. • Locate common types of fire extinguishers in a substation, state their intended use classes, and recognize if an extinguisher is missing or visibly damaged. • Identify eye wash stations, describe when they should be used, and confirm their location and accessibility as part of safety awareness.
Workshop Activities:Focus: Substation Auxiliary Components
• Welcome, objectives, and safety brief.
• Quick walkthrough: LCMS and DCAM panel elements and example alarm decoding
• Charger/DC systems + battery fault signs (nameplate/check examples)
• UPS & network equipment: roles and common front-panel indicators
• Fire panel and extinguisher locate-and-identify exercise.
• Rapid scenario drill: one short incident (e.g., charger alarm or comms loss) — identify, log, and state immediate actions
• Wrap-up, takeaways, and recommended next steps/resources.

201.3Working with DiagramsCourse Title:201.3 Working with Diagrams
Course Structure:Module 1: Diagram - Breaker Control Circuits
• Read and describe breaker control circuits
• Build a system of breaker control circuits
Module 2: Feeder Schematics
• Read and describe feeder schematics
• Continue building relevant circuits
Course Duration:16 Hours0 Minutes16
In-Class Duration:12 Hours0 Minutes12
Workshop Duration:4 Hours0 Minutes4
Course Description:Working with Diagrams teaches Rail Electrical Workers how to read, understand, and use common electrical drawings used in substations and traction systems, starting with breaker control circuits and progressing to feeder schematics. Learners will practice reading and describing circuit elements, following ladder and schematic symbols, and assembling simple systems of related circuits using clear, practical examples and diagrams. Emphasis is on building confidence in interpreting diagrams for safe work planning, troubleshooting communication with maintenance and control staff, and recognizing key components and circuit relationships rather than detailed testing or advanced design.
In-Class Learning Objectives:
• Read and explain the symbols and notations used in ladder diagrams and breaker control circuit drawings. • Identify and describe the function of key components on a breaker control circuit (coil, contacts, interlocks, trip circuits). • Trace current flow through a breaker control circuit to determine how inputs and outputs interact under normal and fault conditions. • Assemble a simple system of related breaker control circuits on paper (or digitally) to show correct interconnections and sequencing. • Read and interpret feeder schematics to identify feeders, protective devices, and connection points to the bus and loads. • Compare breaker control diagrams with feeder schematics to show how control logic and power paths relate. • Use diagrams to support safe work planning by identifying isolation points, visible indicators, and components to report to maintenance or control. • Communicate diagram-based findings clearly to maintenance and traction power control, using component IDs and simple descriptions of observed issues.
Workshop Activities:Focus: Building Circuits

201.4Variations in Substation Equipment ManufacturersCourse Title:201.4 LCMS Views: Variations in Substation Equipment Manufacturers
Course Structure:Comparisons of LCMS views among manufacturers:
• Siemens O&M
• Secheron O&M
• Balfour Beatty O&M
Course Duration:TBD Hours0 Minutes0
In-Class Duration:# Hours0 Minutes0
Workshop Duration:# Hours0 Minutes0
Course Description:This course includes 15 scenarios that show the learning participant how LCMS information about a substation will differ when viewing the data on screen. The variations in navigation, how alarms appear, how phases appear, and downloading will be illustrated in scenarios that cover substation manufacturers: Siemens, Secheron, and Balfour Beatty.
In-Class Learning Objectives:
•Identify key LCMS screen elements (navigation menus, alarm indicators, phase displays, and download controls) for Siemens, Secheron, and Balfour Beatty substation interfaces. • Compare and contrast how navigation workflows differ across Siemens, Secheron, and Balfour Beatty LCMS displays and select the correct navigation path for common tasks. • Interpret alarm presentations (visual cues, severity levels, and contextual details) for each manufacturer and prioritize response actions accordingly. • Explain differences in phase representation (phase labeling, color coding, and phasing diagrams) among the three manufacturers and correctly map displayed phases to field equipment. • Demonstrate how to initiate and complete data downloads (event files, waveform captures, and status logs) from each manufacturer’s interface, including selecting correct export formats. • Validate downloaded data by confirming file integrity and matching file contents to on-screen indicators for Siemens, Secheron, and Balfour Beatty systems. • Troubleshoot common display and data-access issues (missing alarms, incorrect phase display, failed downloads) using manufacturer-specific troubleshooting steps shown in the scenarios. • Apply scenario-based decision-making to select the appropriate vendor-specific procedure for alarm investigation, phase verification, or data extraction in simulated substation events.
Workshop Activities:Focus: LCMS Views - Substation Variations

202.1Maintenance and TestingCourse Title:202.1 Maintenance and Testing
Course Structure:Module 1: AC Breakers
• Inspect, test, and maintain
• Discuss Variations
Module 2: DC Breakers
• Inspect, test, and maintain
• Discuss Variations
Module 3: Transformers
• Inspect, test, and maintain
• Discuss Variations
Module 4: Rectifiers
• Inspect, test, and maintain
• Discuss Variations
Module 5: Protective Relays
• Define protective relays
• Explain future role of the REW Programmer and protective relays
Course Duration:16 Hours0 Minutes16
In-Class Duration:8 Hours0 Minutes8
Workshop Duration:8 Hours0 Minutes8
Course Description:This REW course provides rail electrical workers with practical, hands‑on training to inspect, test, and maintain critical substation equipment across five core modules: AC breakers, DC breakers, transformers, rectifiers, and protective relays. Learners will gain the inspection routines, testing techniques, diagnostic indicators, and maintenance best practices needed to ensure reliable operation and safety, plus an introduction to protective relay functions and the evolving role of the REW Programmer in configuring and supporting protection systems. The course emphasizes real-world procedures, safety checks, and troubleshooting workflows to prepare technicians for day‑to‑day maintenance and commissioning tasks.
In-Class Learning Objectives:
• Identify major components and nameplate data for AC breakers, DC breakers, transformers, rectifiers, and protective relays. • Perform standardized pre‑work visual inspections and safety checks for each equipment type. • Demonstrate basic field test procedures for AC and DC breakers (mechanical operation, insulation/continuity checks). • Conduct transformer and rectifier inspections and basic tests (oil/insulation checks, polarity, output verification) following job‑site checklists. • Interpret common diagnostic indicators and front‑panel alarms for breakers, transformers, rectifiers, UPS, and relay panels. • Explain the primary functions of protective relays and recognize typical trip and alarm indications. • Describe the REW Programmer’s role in relay configuration and relay‑to‑SCADA interactions at a high level. • Use troubleshooting workflows to diagnose and prioritize faults using visual evidence, meter readings, and relay/event data. • Execute and document a basic maintenance action (cleaning, torque check, simple adjustment) using the proper forms and safety controls. • Apply isolation and grounding sequences for safe inspection and testing (sequence steps and required verifications). • Complete an incident/defect report with equipment ID, observed indications, immediate actions taken, and recommended next steps. • Demonstrate safe escalation: when to notify maintenance, traction control, or supervisory staff and how to communicate clear, concise findings.
Workshop Activities:Focus: Maintain and Test
• Welcome, objectives, and safety brief.
• Equipment overview — components, nameplates, safety features
• Activity: Inspect specimen nameplates/components; complete nameplate worksheet.
• Pre‑work inspections, PPE, isolation principles.
• Activity: Run through a 5‑point visual inspection on photos/mock gear.
• Isolation, tagging, grounding, and verification
• Demo and role‑play: isolation/tag/ground sequence using checklist; verification callouts.
• Breaker field tests: AC and DC
• Demo: Mechanical operation, insulation/continuity checks; interpret meter/test readouts.
• Task: Learners interpret sample test logs and mark pass/fail.
• Transformer and rectifier checks.
• Demo: Polarity, insulation/oil indicators, output verification.
• Task: Complete measurement checklist from sample readings.
• Diagnostic indicators, alarms, UPS, relay panel basics.
• Activity: Identify alarm/status on panel screenshots and state immediate actions.
• Protective relay fundamentals and REW Programmer role
• Mini‑lecture: Relay functions, time‑curves, event logs; when to escalate to programmer.
• Task: Read relay display screenshot and summarize trip/alarm.
• Troubleshooting workflow, and prioritization .
• Team scenario: end‑to‑end fault diagnosis using visual evidence, meters, and event logs; create action plan.
• Basic maintenance action with documentation
• Perform one basic maintenance task (cleaning/torque check/simple adjustment) on mock/de‑energized setup or document performed action from scenario.
• Complete work‑order entry with steps, measurements, parts, attachments, and recommendations.
• Escalation briefing and close‑out
• Each team delivers a 2‑3 minute escalation/maintenance briefing; peer + instructor feedback.
• Debrief, post‑test/confidence poll, distribute job aids, next steps.

202.2Traction Power Substation Maintenance StandardCourse Title:202.2 Traction Power Substation Maintenance Standard
Course Structure:Module 1: Traction Power Maintenance Standard
• Become familiar with the Sound Transit Traction Power Substation Maintenance Standard
• Work orders
o Introduce the utilization of tablets / shop computers and EAMS system for work order completion entry (Procedural guidance for W.O.’s will follow in 301.1 Substation Procedural Review Part 2.)
• Scenario-based learning
o Maintenance: DC Breakers
1. Locate procedures to perform
2. Record steps taken during maintenance
3. Record Outcomes
• Scenario-based learning
o Maintenance: Relays (The maintenance of relays checklist)
1. Locate procedures to perform
2. Record steps taken during maintenance
3. Record Outcomes
• Scenario-based learning
o Maintenance: Batteries
1. Locate procedures to perform
2. Record steps taken during maintenance
3. Record Outcomes
Course Duration:8 Hours0 Minutes8
In-Class Duration:2 Hours0 Minutes2
Workshop Duration:6 Hours0 Minutes6
Course Description:This course familiarizes Rail Electrical Workers with the Sound Transit Traction Power Substation Maintenance Standard and practical maintenance workflows, including using tablets/shop computers and the EAMS for work order entry (procedural guidance continued in 301.1 Substation Procedural Review Part 2). Through scenario-based exercises, learners will locate and follow approved procedures, perform maintenance tasks on DC breakers, protective relays, and batteries, and accurately record steps taken and outcomes for each job. Emphasizing safety, compliance, and clear documentation, the course prepares technicians to execute standardized maintenance work and reliably capture evidence of completed work in the asset management system.
In-Class Learning Objectives:
•Describe the purpose and scope of the Sound Transit Traction Power Substation Maintenance Standard. • Interpret a maintenance work order to identify required procedures, safety controls, and required tools. • Locate the correct procedural checklist for DC breaker maintenance and explain key steps before starting work. • Accurately record maintenance steps, measurements, and observations for a DC breaker work order. • Locate the relay maintenance checklist, perform required inspection/test steps conceptually, and log outcomes. • Identify the correct battery maintenance procedure, note visible signs of battery issues, and document results. • Complete a clear work-order outcome entry that records actions taken, test results, parts used, and recommended follow‑up. • Apply required safety and compliance steps (isolation, tagging, PPE) and note them in the work-order record. • Demonstrate how to escalate unusual findings or defects via the EAMS/work-order comments and appropriate supervisory channels.
Workshop Activities:Focus: Maintain and Test
• Welcome, objectives, and safety brief.
• Activity: Guided tour of the substation using the TPSS Maintenance Standard PDF (highlight critical sections: safety, documentation, acceptance criteria).
• Work-order interpretation and preparation.
• Walkthrough: Identify required safety controls, tools, parts, and estimated duration from the WO.
• Task: Interpret a provided WO and list required PPE, lock/tag steps, and tools on worksheet.
• DC breaker procedural checklist and hands-on documentation
• Instructor demo: Locate DC breaker checklist, review key pre-work and isolation steps.
• Practical exercise (teams): Perform a checklist-based visual inspection on a mock/de-energized breaker or photos/simulators; take sample measurements and record steps on the WO template.
• Deliverable: Completed DC breaker inspection log and WO notes.
• Relay maintenance checklist and event interpretation.
• Demo: Locate relay checklist, review typical inspection/test steps and expected outcomes.
• Exercise: Interpret two relay screenshots/event logs, note actions, and log conceptual test results.
• Battery maintenance procedure and inspection.
• Demo: Battery checks, visible degradation signs, safety controls, and documentation fields.
• Task: Inspect sample battery photos or de-energized cell, record findings and suggested follow-up in WO.
• Isolation, tagging, grounding, and safety documentation
• Instructor-led sequence: Isolation/tagging/verification and required documentation entries.
• Role-play: Teams run through isolation steps using checklist and create the required WO entries and permit notes.
• Escalation and close-out
• Teach: How to record anomalies, add EAMS comments, attach photos/test logs, and draft a concise supervisory notification.
• Exercise: Given a simulated abnormal finding, learners add comments/attachments in EAMS and practice a 60–90 sec escalation brief.
• Integrated scenario
• Team scenario: Fulfill mini-work order from open → inspection → basic maintenance action → document → escalate/close.
• Deliverable: Completed WO in EAMS, incident log, and verbal escalation.
• Debrief, Q&A, and lessons learned
• Instructor feedback on key errors, documentation quality, and safety adherence.
• Post-test or confidence poll, distribution of one-page job aids and links to the Standard and 301.1 Procedural Review Part 2.

203.1Preparing to Work on the Overhead Contact SystemCourse Title:203.1 Preparing to Work on the Overhead Contact System
Course Structure:Module 1: Working at Heights – Fall Protection
• Describe and explain safety procedures for working at heights and fall protection
Module 2: Overview on Switching, Tagging and Return to Service (Energized and De-energized)
• Introduction: Express energized and de-energized as it relates to the OCS
• Switching and Tagging Instructions
• Instructions on Power Interruptions and Return to Service
Module 3: Rigging
• Explain specialized methods, equipment, and labor used to lift, move, position, and secure heavy electrical components and tensioned wires.
Module 4: Bucket Rescue
• In brief, describe the nature of bucket rescue and why it is important
Module 5: Shorting and Grounding (Energize / De-energize)
• Detail the critical safety procedures performed during a de-energizing (power-down) action used to protect yourself and others from high-voltage DC or AC systems
Module 6: Confined Spaces
• Explain (briefly) the aspects of working in confined spaces
• Reference existing ST/KCM training in the training jacket
Course Duration:5 Hours0 Minutes5
In-Class Duration:2 Hours0 Minutes2
Workshop Duration:3 Hours0 Minutes3
Course Description:This course prepares rail electrical workers to safely perform overhead contact system (OCS) work by teaching essential safety practices, switching and tagging procedures, and hands‑on readiness skills. Modules cover fall protection and working at heights; OCS‑specific switching, tagging, power‑interruption, and return‑to‑service protocols for energized and de‑energized work; rigging techniques for lifting and securing heavy components and tensioned wires; bucket rescue awareness and response; shorting and grounding procedures to protect personnel during de‑energizing and re‑energizing; and confined‑space considerations with references to existing Sound Transit/King County Metro training. Emphasizing practical procedures, hazard controls, and compliance, the course readies crews to plan, execute, and document safe OCS maintenance and emergency actions.
In-Class Learning Objectives:
• Describe required fall‑protection equipment, anchor/select/load limits, and rescue considerations for working at heights on the OCS. • Demonstrate correct use of personal fall‑arrest systems, lanyards, harness inspection, and pre‑work safety checks. • Define “energized” vs. “de‑energized” for OCS work and state when each condition applies. • Interpret switching and tagging instructions for OCS tasks and identify required permissions, lockout/tagout steps, and documentation. • Explain procedures for planned power interruptions and safe return‑to‑service, including notification and verification steps. • Identify common rigging gear and methods used for lifting, positioning, and securing heavy OCS components and tensioned wires. • Select appropriate rigging hardware and describe basic rigging safety checks and hand signals for team lifts. • Summarize the purpose and basic sequence of a bucket rescue and list immediate actions to initiate a rescue safely. • List critical shorting and grounding steps for de‑energizing/energizing OCS equipment and explain how they protect personnel. • Demonstrate how to verify grounds/shorts and document verification per procedure. • Describe confined‑space hazards relevant to OCS work, entry controls, and required permits/communications. • Locate and reference applicable Sound Transit / King County Metro training and procedural materials in the training jacket for follow‑up and compliance.
Workshop Activities:Focus: OCS Work Prep
• Welcome, objectives, safety brief
• Fall protection fundamentals
• Demo: Harness inspection/donning and anchor selection; hands‑on harness pre‑use checklist.
• Energized vs. de‑energized & switching/tagging basics
• Walkthrough switching/tagging steps, required permissions, and sample switching order interpretation exercise
• Shorting & grounding procedures
• Demo: Grounding sequence and verification; learners complete a ground‑verification practice using simulated equipment or checklists.
• Rigging basics for OCS components
• Show common slings/shackles/hitches; team selects rigging plan for a sample lift and reviews hand signals/safety checks.
• Bucket rescue overview
• Brief flowchart of rescue steps, roles, and immediate actions; short role‑play on initiating a rescue and calling resources.
• Confined spaces & procedural references
• Quick review of confined‑space entry controls and where to find ST/KCM training and permits in the training jacket.
• Integrated wrap-up and documentation
• Collect completed worksheets, ground verification forms, and one short escalation statement per team; distribute one‑page job aids.

203.2Inspection and MaintenanceCourse Title:203.2 Inspection and Maintenance
Course Structure:Module 1: Contact Wire (Cable)
• Tools for working on the contact wire
• Wire specifications and wear limits
• Height specifications
• Staggering details
• Pantograph arcing issues
Module 2: Supporting Structure
• Tools for working on supporting structures
• Messenger wire specifications and wear limits
• Height specifications
• Hangers
• Insulators
• Poles
• Pole Foundation
• Fasteners torque requirement
• Guy wires
Module 3: Electrical and Sectionalizing Components
• Insulators
• Feeder Cables
• Disconnects
• Overlaps
• Lightening arrestors
• Catenary insulators
• Arcing horn
• Bypasses
• Floating Bridge Expansion Joints
Course Duration:16 Hours0 Minutes16
In-Class Duration:8 Hours0 Minutes8
Workshop Duration:8 Hours0 Minutes8
Course Description:This course trains Rail Electrical Workers to inspect, maintain, and document overhead contact system (OCS) components with a focus on safe, standards‑based field practice. Through three modules—Contact Wire, Supporting Structure, and Electrical & Sectionalizing Components—learners will become proficient with the tools and procedures for assessing contact wire condition, wear limits, height and staggering requirements, and pantograph arcing issues; inspecting messenger wire, hangers, insulators, poles, foundations, fasteners, and guy wires to torque and condition standards; and evaluating insulators, feeder cables, disconnects, overlaps, surge/arrest devices, arcing horns, bypasses, and expansion joints. Emphasizing hands‑on inspection routines, measurable acceptance criteria, troubleshooting indicators, and clear work‑order documentation, the course readies crews to perform routine maintenance, identify defects requiring escalation, and support reliable OCS operation.
In-Class Learning Objectives:
• Identify and select the proper tools and PPE for contact‑wire inspection and maintenance. • Measure contact‑wire diameter and wear, compare to specification limits, and decide accept/replace actions. • Verify contact‑wire height and staggering against standards and record deviations. • Recognize pantograph arcing signs and document likely causes and immediate mitigation steps. • Perform a hands‑on contact‑wire visual inspection and complete the contact‑wire checklist. • Identify rigging and tools used for supporting‑structure work and demonstrate basic safe handling procedures. • Measure messenger‑wire condition and wear, and assess against acceptance criteria. • Inspect hangers, insulators, poles, foundations, fasteners, and guy wires for common defects and torque fasteners to specified values. • Distinguish acceptable vs. degraded pole‑foundation and guy‑wire conditions and note required escalations. • Locate and identify electrical/sectionalizing components (feeders, disconnects, overlaps, arcing horns, bypasses, expansion joints). • interpret common front‑panel or physical indicators of failure for insulators, feeder cables, and disconnects. • Inspect surge/arrest devices and catenary insulators for visible damage and document findings. • Perform a basic assessment of floating bridge expansion joints and identify signs of mechanical or electrical distress. • Use standardized work‑order templates to record inspection steps, measurements, outcomes, and recommended follow‑up. • Prioritize defects requiring immediate isolation/escalation and prepare a concise escalation brief for maintenance or engineering. • Apply troubleshooting steps to common OCS faults and propose short‑term containment and long‑term repair recommendations.
Workshop Activities:Focus: OCS Inspection and Maintenance
• Welcome, objectives, safety brief
• Tools, PPE, and inspection kits
• Activity: Tool / PPE station: Learners choose equipment from kits; instructor verifies choices and common mistakes.
• Contact‑wire specs, wear, height & staggering
• Demo: Caliper / gauge use and height / stagger measurement method.
• Activity: Wire‑measurement drill on sample sections; record decisions on worksheet.
• Contact‑wire inspection & pantograph arcing
• Activity: Hands‑on visual inspection on de‑energized mockup or detailed photos; complete contact‑wire checklist.
• Photo analysis: Pantograph arcing cases — document causes and immediate mitigations.
• Messenger wire, hangers, insulators, and supporting‑structure inspection
• Stations: Messenger wear, hanger condition, insulator checks; learners rotate and complete station worksheets.
• Poles, foundations, fasteners, guy wires, torque practice
• Activity: Inspect sample poles/foundations (photos/mock), hands‑on torque practice on test bolts to specified values, record readings.
• Electrical & sectionalizing components identification and failure indicators
• Scavenger Hunt / Recognition: Locate feeders, disconnects, overlaps, arcing horns, bypasses, expansion joints (mock/photo set).
• Interpret front‑panel indicators and common physical fault signs; log probable causes.
• Surge / arrest, catenary insulators, and floating bridge expansion joint assessment
• Demo and hands‑on/photo checks; complete assessment checklist for expansion joints.
• Documentation and work‑order practice
• Activity: using standardized WO template, enter inspection steps, measurements, photos, parts, and recommended follow‑up from earlier stations.
• Prioritization, escalation brief & troubleshooting scenario
• Team exercise: Rank defects from a mixed set, create isolation plan, and deliver a 90‑second escalation brief to maintenance / controller.
• Troubleshooting: Run a short simulated fault scenario, propose immediate containment actions and long‑term repair plan.
• Wrap up, post‑workshop poll, handouts, next steps.

203.3TensioningCourse Title:203.3 Tensioning
Course Structure:Module 1: Tensioning Maintenance and Inspection
• Constant tension and auto tensioning fundamentals
• Tools for tensioning
• Calculations and specifications for tensioning
• How to tighten and adjust cables
• How to conduct inspections
• Understanding tensioning maintenance protocol
• Seasonal adjustments to tensioning
Course Duration:4 Hours0 Minutes4
In-Class Duration:2 Hours0 Minutes2
Video Demonstration:2 Hours0 Minutes2
Course Description:This course trains Rail Electrical Workers in the principles and practice of OCS tensioning, covering constant‑tension and auto‑tensioning fundamentals, required tools, tension calculations and specification checks, and safe cable tightening and adjustment techniques. Learners will practice inspection methods, apply tensioning maintenance protocols, perform seasonal adjustment procedures, and complete hands‑on exercises using tensioning equipment and measurement tools. Emphasizing safety, documentation, and accuracy, the course prepares technicians to diagnose tension-related issues, execute approved adjustments, and record compliant inspection and maintenance outcomes.
In-Class Learning Objectives:
• Explain constant‑tension and auto‑tensioning principles and how each system maintains OCS wire geometry. • Identify common tensioning tools and equipment, describe their purpose, and perform pre‑use safety checks. • Calculate target tension using provided formulas and specification tables and verify values against nameplate/range limits. • Select the correct tensioning method (constant vs. auto) for a given scenario and justify the choice. • Demonstrate safe cable tightening and adjustment techniques on a mock setup, including proper use of grips and turning devices. • Conduct a tension inspection: measure tension, record readings, compare to specs, and note deviations. • Recognize common tension‑related defects (sags, broken strands, uneven staggering) and determine immediate containment actions. • Apply seasonal adjustment procedures and explain why temperature changes affect tensioning decisions. • Follow tensioning maintenance protocol steps, including isolation, permits, PPE, and tagging requirements. • Complete standardized inspection and maintenance documentation with calculated values, actions taken, and recommended follow‑up. • Prioritize tensioning issues for escalation versus routine repair and prepare a concise escalation summary for engineering/maintenance.
Video Prompts to Follow:Focus: Tensioning Maintenance and Inspection
Shot: Instructor standing by OCS mockup with tensioning gear. Prompt: Introduce constant‑tension and auto‑tensioning and state the goal: Maintain wire geometry and pantograph contact. Action: Show labeled diagram overlay comparing systems.
Shot: Diagram showing how constant‑tension spring and auto‑tensioning mechanism react to temperature / load. Prompt: Explain step‑by‑step how each system absorbs length change and keeps sag/stagger within spec. Action: Zoom to spring/compressor action and a temperature scale.
Shot: Workbench with calipers, tension meter, grips, turnbuckles, clamps, slings, torque wrench. Prompt: Name each tool, describe purpose, and demonstrate a pre‑use inspection checklist (damage, calibration, serial/label). Action: Closeups of inspection points and an onscreen checklist ticked.
Shot: Nameplate / spec verification...Learner reading a wire/anchor nameplate and a specification table on tablet. Prompt: Show how to read nameplate/range limits and cross‑check against spec tables before calculations. Action: Highlight values and tap to populate calculation form.
Shot: Tension calculation demo...Split screen of instructor writing formula and tablet auto‑calc. Prompt: Walk through calculating target tension using given formula and sample numbers; verify result against nameplate limits. Action: Display final numeric result with pass/fail indicator.
Shot: Safe tightening technique...Hands-on demo on mock cable: install grips, attach turnbuckle, use tensioning tool. Prompt: Demonstrate safe cable tightening: correct grip placement, body position, controlled turns, and clear verbal commands. Action: Show correct vs incorrect technique, call out hazards.
Shot: Tension measurement procedure...Operator using tension meter on mock cable; screen shows reading. Prompt: Measure tension step-by-step, record readings on inspection form, and show comparing to spec with pass/fail callout. Action: Overlay of recorded values and signature block.
Shot: Inspection recording workflow...Tablet E‑form being filled: location, measurement, photos, notes. Prompt: Capture photo evidence, annotate deviations, and complete required fields for the work order. Action: Demonstrate attaching photos and submitting draft.
Shot: Defect recognition...Closeups of sagging wire, broken strands, uneven staggering, pantograph arcing marks. Prompt: Identify each defect, explain probable causes, and state immediate containment actions (temporary shoring, restricting traffic, tagging). Action: Label each defect and show an immediate mitigation step.
Shot: Pantograph arcing troubleshooting...Pantograph head closeup and contact wire with burn marks (photo/video). Prompt: Document arcing signs, list likely root causes, and recommend immediate mitigations and follow‑up tests. Action: Annotate photo with likely causes and next steps.
Shot: Seasonal adjustment explanation...Temperature/time-lapse overlay on wire sag diagram. Prompt: Explain how temperature affects tension, demonstrate computing seasonal setpoints, and show adjustment window checks. Action: Compare cold vs hot target tensions and required actions.
Shot: Protocol and safety sequence...Checklist flowchart: isolate → permit → PPE → tag → adjust → verify → restore. Prompt: Walk through tensioning maintenance protocol including isolation, permits, PPE, and tagging requirements. Action: Role‑play a short permit sign‑off and crew brief.
Shot: Ground/nearby systems caution...Nearby OCS /l ins labeled; worker confirming clearances. Prompt: Demonstrate verifying adjacent systems are safe and communications with traction control before tensioning. Action: Show radio call and confirmed clearance.
Shot: Troubleshooting scenario end‑to‑end...Simulated fault scenario from discovery to containment to repair recommendation. Prompt: Narrate applying the troubleshooting workflow: observe → measure → analyze → contain → repair plan. Show short‑term containment and long‑term repair options. Action: Show team executing containment and drafting repair ticket.
Shot: Key takeaways...Instructor on-camera with job aids visible. Prompt: Recap crucial safety checks, measurement best practices, documentation musts, and when to escalate. Provide links to reference materials and job aids. Action: Display downloadable resources and contact points for support.

203.4Overhead Contact System (OCS) Sectionalizing Course Title:203.4 Overhead Contact System (OCS) Sectionalizing
Course Structure:Module 1: Sectionalizing Drawings – Gaining Understanding
• Describe the OCS in terms of smaller, electrically independent sections
• Explain how section insulators and disconnect switches are used to isolate specific portions of the track
• Describe how isolation techniques allow for maintenance crews to work safely on one part of the railway system while power remains active in other parts of the system
Course Duration:8 Hours0 Minutes8
In-Class Duration:4 Hours0 Minutes4
Video Demonstration:4 Hours0 Minutes4
Course Description:This REW course teaches rail electrical workers how to read and apply OCS sectionalizing drawings to manage electrically independent track sections safely during maintenance. Learners will interpret sectionalizing diagrams, identify section insulators and disconnect switches, and practice isolation techniques used to de‑energize and secure specific track segments while allowing adjacent sections to remain live. Emphasizing practical procedures, risk controls, and clear documentation, the course prepares crews to plan safe work boundaries, execute verified isolations, coordinate with traction control, and restore service with confidence.
In-Class Learning Objectives:
• Explain the concept of OCS sectionalizing and identify electrically independent sections on system diagrams. • Read and interpret sectionalizing drawings, symbols, and legends (section insulators, disconnects, overlaps, feed points). • Locate section insulators and disconnect switches in the field using drawings and GIS/site references. • Describe the functional role of section insulators and disconnects in isolating track segments for maintenance. • Determine required isolation boundaries for a given maintenance task and produce a clear isolation plan. • Apply lockout/tagout and isolation procedures specific to sectionalized OCS work, including required permits and verification steps. • Coordinate isolation actions with traction control and other stakeholders, including notification, scheduling, and re‑energization sequencing. • Perform verification checks to confirm an isolated section is de‑energized (visual, meter, grounding/shorting as required) and document results. • Draft accurate work orders and isolation checklists that record equipment IDs, switch positions, verification readings, and safety controls. • Execute simulated isolation scenarios: implement the plan, verify isolation, manage temporary boundaries, and restore service. • Identify risks and failure modes associated with sectionalizing (incorrect switch position, accidental re‑energization, overlap faults) and apply mitigation measures. • Prepare and deliver concise escalation and handover briefs that summarize isolation status, outstanding risks, and next steps for maintenance or operations.
Video Prompts to Follow:Focus: Tensioning Maintenance and Inspection
Shot: Instructor in front of sectionalizing diagram on screen. Prompt: Introduce OCS sectionalizing: explain electrically independent sections and why sectionalizing enables safe localized work while adjacent sections remain live. Action: Point to sections on diagram; overlay labeled zones.

Prompt: Show how to verify a component in the field using drawing coordinates/site markers and physical identifiers (tag numbers/nameplates). Action: Closeups of tag/nameplate, GPS waypoint overlay.
Shot: Isolation demo…Sequence of isolating one section while others remain energized. Prompt: Explain how section insulators and disconnects interrupt continuity and create safe work boundaries. Action: Color energized vs de-energized sections; show worker area isolated.
Shot: Isolation planning: Checklist creation...Instructor filling an isolation plan template on tablet. Prompt: Walk through determining isolation boundaries for a sample maintenance task and populate a clear isolation plan (equipment IDs, switches, verification steps). Action: Zoom to filled fields.

Prompt: Demonstrate lockout/tagout and permit steps specific to sectionalized OCS work, including required signatures and communication steps. Action: Apply tag, sign permit, hand copy to control center.
Shot: Coordination with Traction Power Controller...Simulated call trainee on radio/phone briefing traction control with plan summary. Prompt: Model coordination: notify traction control, confirm outage window, request switching, and agree verification steps and re‑energization sequencing. Action: Show script overlay of key call points.
Shot: Switch operation and verification: meter use...Operator changes switch position (de‑energized scenario) and uses a voltmeter. Prompt: Demonstrate safe switch operation procedure and perform verification checks (visual confirmation, meter readings, grounding/shorting if required). Action: Display meter readout and checklist tick.
Shot: Grounding/shorting verification demonstration...Crew installs temporary grounds and verifies continuity. Prompt: Show proper shorting/grounding sequence, verification method, and documentation of readings. Action: Closeups of clamp attachment and recorded values.
Shot: Work‑order & checklist documentation: tablet capture...Tablet screen capturing equipment IDs, switch positions, photos, and verification readings. Prompt: Demonstrate completing a work order/isolation checklist with photos and verification signatures for auditability. Action: Attach photo, enter meter value, submit.
Shot: Isolation scenario: team execution...Time‑lapse of team executing isolation plan from briefing to verification. Prompt: Run an end‑to‑end simulated isolation: implement plan, verify de‑energized status, set boundaries, and hand over to maintenance. Action: Show each checklist step checked off.
Shot: Re‑energization sequence...Team performing restore checklist and notifying traction control for re‑energization. Prompt: Demonstrate safe return‑to‑service steps: clear tools, remove grounds, verify switch positions, and confirm with control before restoring power. Action: Show final verification and system status change.
Shot: Risks and failure modes...Show potential errors (wrong switch, missing tag, overlap fault). Prompt: Identify common failure modes and mitigation measures: double‑check IDs, independent verification, use of overlaps, and immediate stop/notify procedures. Action: Overlay mitigation checklist for each case.
Shot: Escalation and handover brief...Trainee delivers 60–90 sec briefing to supervisor with photos and WO summary. Prompt: Model a concise escalation/handover: equipment ID, isolation status, verification results, outstanding risks, and recommended next steps. Action: Show on‑screen briefing template.

201.1AC Power Systems Inspection and MaintenanceCourse Title:201.1 AC Power Systems Inspection and Maintenance
Part 4: AC Power Systems Switchgear
Course Structure:Module 1: Maintain AC Power Systems Switchgear
• Explain and maintain switchgear for AC Power Systems
Module 2: AC Power Systems Disconnect Switches (Load & Non-Load)
• Explain and maintain disconnect switches (load and non-load)
Course Duration:4 Hours0 Minutes4
Course Description:This course helps the REW become more familiar with AC switchgear and disconnect switches used in traction and power systems by combining an explanation of component functions and operating principles with practical guidance for inspection, testing ,and maintenance. Topics include types and construction of switchgear, load and no‑load disconnect switch behavior, earthing/disconnect arrangements, mechanisms and contact systems, common failure modes, routine mechanical and electrical checks, operational testing, safe isolation and earthing procedures, and site‑specific maintenance tasks (adjustment, cleaning, contact care and minor repairs). Emphasis is on interpreting test results, documenting findings, applying safe work practices and escalation routes, and preparing learners for subsequent hands‑on switchgear maintenance workshops.
Course Outcomes:Technicians will be able to explain the functions and operating principles of AC switchgear and load/no‑load disconnect switches, identify common failure modes and earthing/disconnect arrangements, perform structured visual, mechanical and electrical inspections, carry out basic operational tests and routine maintenance tasks (adjustment, cleaning, contact care), apply correct isolation and earthing procedures for safe work, interpret test results to assess condition, accurately document findings and test data, and escalate or recommend corrective actions to specialist teams while being prepared for subsequent hands‑on switchgear maintenance workshops.
Learning Objectives:• Explain the functions, types and basic construction of AC switchgear and disconnect switches and correctly label three example components on a diagram. • Differentiate load vs no‑load disconnect switch behavior and state two typical applications for each. • Identify common earthing/disconnect arrangements and select the correct isolation sequence for a given single‑line scenario. • List five common failure modes of switchgear/disconnects and match each to its typical visual or test indicator. • Describe how to perform a structured visual and mechanical inspection using a provided checklist and record all defects found. • Measure insulation resistance and contact resistance using site test equipment, record readings, and compare them to specified acceptance criteria. • Explain how to conduct basic operational tests (open/close operations, interlock checks) and log timing or functional results against pass/fail criteria. • Apply correct isolation and earthing procedures on a mock or diagrammed task and verify sequence compliance. • Carry out routine maintenance tasks (adjustment, cleaning, contact care, minor repairs) per site procedure and demonstrate completed work on one component. • Interpret test and inspection data to determine equipment condition and classify the item as Acceptable / Requires Repair / Unsafe. • Complete accurate inspection and test reports, including readings, observations, actions taken and recommended next steps. • Describe how/when to escalate protection, safety, or major fault conditions by creating and submitting an incident/escalation report with required technical details for specialist follow-up.

Part 3 DC Power Systems Circuit Breakers & Protective Devices - Explanation
Course Structure:Module 1: DC Power Systems: Circuit Breakers & Protective Devices - Explanation
• Explain circuit breakers and protective devices
Module 2: DC Power Systems: Circuit Breakers & Protective Devices - Maintenance
• Maintain circuit breakers and protective devices
Module 3: DC Power Systems: Switchgear
• Maintain DC switchgear
Module 4: DC Power Systems: Disconnect Switches (Load & No-Load)
• Maintain disconnect switches (load and no-load)
Module 5: DC Power Systems: Rectifier - Explain and Maintain
• Explain and maintain rectifier
Course Duration:4 Hours30 Minutes4.5
Course Description:This REW learning course explains DC circuit breakers, protective devices, switchgear, load and no‑load disconnect switches, and rectifier systems used in traction and depot networks. Learners study device types, operating principles, common failure modes, and protection/coordination concepts. The course covers structured inspection, testing and routine maintenance tasks for breakers, switchgear, disconnects and rectifiers. Emphasis is also placed on safe isolation and earthing, correct test procedures, interpreting diagnostic results, documenting findings, and recognizing when to escalate to specialists. Practical examples and exercises prepare REWs for subsequent hands‑on maintenance activities.
Course Outcomes:Technicians will be able to describe DC circuit breakers, protective devices, switchgear, disconnect switches and rectifier systems and explain their operating principles. They will identify common failure modes and basic protection/coordination concepts. Learners will perform structured inspections, run standard tests, and carry out routine maintenance tasks using correct procedures. They will apply safe isolation and earthing, interpret diagnostic results, and document findings accurately. Finally, they will recognize faults that require specialist escalation and prepare clear reports for follow‑up.
Learning Objectives:• Describe types and operating principles of DC circuit breakers, protective devices, switchgear, disconnect switches and rectifier systems and label major components on a diagram. • Identify five common failure modes for DC breakers, switchgear, disconnects and rectifiers and match each to typical causes or indicators. • Explain basic protection and coordination concepts and determine appropriate device settings for a given single‑line scenario. • Locate breakers, trip circuits, earth/ground points and rectifier connections on single‑line diagrams and equipment nameplates. • Perform a structured visual and mechanical inspection of a DC breaker or disconnect using a provided checklist and record all defects. • Carry out standard electrical tests (continuity, insulation resistance, contact/milliohm, trip‑circuit verification) and log measured values. • Execute basic rectifier checks (output voltage, DC ripple, diode/bridge functional test) and compare results to acceptance criteria. • Apply correct isolation and grounding/earthing sequences on a mock task and verify compliance with site procedure. • Interpret diagnostic and test data to classify equipment condition as Acceptable / Requires Repair / Unsafe and justify the classification with measured evidence. • Complete standardized inspection and test reports with readings, observations, maintenance actions and recommended follow‑up. • Escalate complex or unsafe faults by preparing and submitting an incident/escalation report containing required technical details for specialist review. • Demonstrate one routine maintenance task (e.g., contact cleaning, lubrication, tightness check) on a component per site procedure.

201.1AC Power Systems Inspection and MaintenanceCourse Title:201.1 AC Power Systems Inspection and Maintenance - Part 5: AC Power Systems Traction Rectifier Transformer
Part 5: AC Power Systems Traction Rectifier Transformer
Course Structure:Module 1: Traction Rectifier Transformer
• Explain traction rectifier transformer (6 pulse vs. 12 pulse)
Module 2: Rectifier - Explain and Maintain
• Explain and maintain AC power systems rectifier.
Course Duration:4 Hours0 Minutes4
Course Description:In this course, the REW will be given an explanation of traction rectifier transformers and the associated rectifier equipment used to convert AC supply for traction, comparing 6‑pulse and 12‑pulse topologies, their harmonic characteristics, and installation considerations. Learners will study transformer and rectifier construction, operating principles, protection and cooling arrangements, common failure modes, and harmonic/neutral‑current issues. Additionally, participants will receive guidance in practical inspection, diagnostic testing, and routine maintenance tasks for both transformers and rectifier assemblies (insulation checks, ratio/polarity, thermal monitoring, diode/bridge testing, cooling and tap‑changer care). Emphasis is on safe isolation and earthing for testing, interpreting test results, documenting findings, and recognizing when to escalate complex faults to protection or specialist teams. Worked examples and exercises will take place to prepare participants for subsequent hands‑on maintenance modules.
Course Outcomes:Technicians will be able to explain the purpose and operating principles of traction rectifier transformers and rectifier assemblies, compare 6‑pulse and 12‑pulse topologies and their harmonic effects, identify transformer and rectifier construction features, protection/cooling arrangements and common failure modes, perform structured visual inspections and basic diagnostic tests (insulation, ratio/polarity, thermal checks, diode/bridge tests), interpret test results and harmonic/neutral‑current indicators, apply correct isolation and earthing for safe testing, document findings and test data, and escalate complex or unsafe faults to protection or specialist teams while being prepared for subsequent hands‑on maintenance modules.
Learning Objectives:• Describe the purpose and operating principles of traction rectifier transformers and rectifier assemblies and correctly label major components on a diagram. • Compare 6‑pulse and 12‑pulse rectifier topologies and list three differences in harmonic output and neutral current behavior. • Identify transformer and rectifier construction features, protection and cooling arrangements, and match five common failure modes to their typical causes. • Perform a structured visual inspection of a rectifier transformer/assembly using a provided checklist and record all defects found. • Measure insulation resistance and transformer ratio/polarity using site test equipment, record readings, and verify they meet specified limits. • Conduct thermal monitoring checks (thermometer/IR) and log temperatures, flagging readings outside normal operating ranges. • Test rectifier diodes/bridges with appropriate test procedures, record pass/fail results, and isolate faulty components for escalation. • Measure and interpret neutral‑current or harmonic indicators from provided measurement data and classify the severity of harmonic-related issues. • Apply correct isolation and earthing sequences on a diagrammed task or mock setup and verify compliance with site procedure. • Interpret diagnostic and test data to classify equipment condition as Acceptable / Requires Repair / Unsafe and recommend next actions. • Complete standardized inspection and test reports with readings, observations, actions taken and recommended follow‑up. • Escalate complex or unsafe faults by creating and submitting an incident/escalation report containing required technical details for protection or specialist teams.

201.2DC Power Systems: Inspection and MaintenanceCourse Title:201.2 DC Power Systems Inspection and Maintenance - Part 1: DC Power Systems Theory
Part 1: DC Power Systems TheoryCourse Structure:Introduction
Module 1: Review of DC Theory
• Examine the theory and principles of direct current power systems
Course Duration:1 Hour0 Minutes1
Course Description:This course reviews the theory and principles of direct current (DC) power systems relevant to railway traction and depot networks, reinforcing fundamentals such as voltage, current, resistance, Ohm’s law, DC circuit theory, conductors and return paths, battery and storage systems, rectification, and power conversion. This course also explains grounding/earthing, protection schemes, and common fault types, while linking these concepts to practical inspection and maintenance tasks by covering measurement techniques, interpretation of DC readings, fault diagnosis, mitigation strategies, safe isolation practices for DC equipment, and worked examples that prepare REWs for subsequent hands‑on inspection and maintenance modules.
Course Outcomes:Technicians will be able to explain core DC concepts (voltage, current, resistance, Ohm’s law, conductors and return paths), describe battery/storage, rectification, and DC conversion principles. They will also be able to begin outlining grounding/earthing and common protection schemes; while performing and interpreting essential DC measurements, in addition to applying circuit theory to diagnose typical DC faults, recommend appropriate mitigation actions, and demonstrate correct isolation and safe work practices for DC equipment - all of which will prepare learners for subsequent hands‑on inspection and maintenance tasks.
Learning Objectives:• Explain voltage, current and resistance and solve three basic Ohm’s law problems for DC circuits. • Identify conductor and return path types and trace current flow on a provided circuit diagram. • Describe battery and energy‑storage components and state two performance indicators to check during inspections. • Explain rectification and DC‑DC conversion principles and label a simple rectifier and converter on a diagram. • Outline common grounding/earthing arrangements and select the correct earthing method for a given DC system scenario. • Describe typical DC protection schemes (fuses, DC breakers, relays) and match each to its protective function. • Measure DC voltage, current and resistance with a multimeter, record readings, and compare them to specified reference values. • Perform a battery state‑of‑charge and health check using provided test procedures and record results. • Diagnose three common DC faults (short, open, high resistance/poor return) from measurement data and propose immediate mitigation steps. • Apply correct isolation and earthing sequences on a mock or diagrammed task and demonstrate compliance with site procedure. • Complete an inspection report including measurements, diagnosis, actions taken and recommended follow‑up. • Escalate unsafe conditions or complex faults by preparing an incident report containing the required technical details for specialist review.

201.2DC Power Systems Inspection and MaintenanceCourse Title:201.2 DC Power Systems Inspection and Maintenance - Part 2: DC Power Systems Instrument Transformers
Part 2 DC Power Systems Instrument Transformers
Course Structure:Module 1: DC Power Systems Instrument Transformers
• Explain, inspect, and maintain instrument transformers
Module 2: DC Power Systems Auxiliary Transformers - Maintenance
• Explain, inspect, and maintain auxiliary transformers
Course Duration:2 Hours30 Minutes2.5
Course Description:This course covers instrument and auxiliary transformers used in DC traction power systems, explaining their purpose, construction and operating principles, and providing practical guidance for inspection, testing and routine maintenance. Learners will examine DC instrument transformer types (shunts, DC current transformers, and associated secondary circuits), auxiliary transformer roles, common failure modes, installation and wiring considerations, and routine diagnostic checks (insulation, polarity/ratio where applicable, burden and secondary circuit integrity). The course emphasizes correct isolation and earthing procedures for safe testing, interpretation of diagnostic results, documentation of findings, and escalation routes, with worked examples and exercises to prepare participants for subsequent hands‑on inspection and maintenance activities.
Course Outcomes:Technicians will be able to explain the purpose, construction, and operating principles of DC instrument transformers (shunts, DC current transformers) and auxiliary transformers. They will also be prepared to perform structured visual inspections and routine diagnostic checks (insulation, polarity/ratio where applicable, burden and secondary circuit integrity); identify common failure modes and installation/wiring defects; carry out basic maintenance and site‑appropriate tests with correct isolation and earthing; interpret test results to assess condition and performance; accurately document findings and test data; and escalate or recommend corrective actions to protection or specialist teams - all of which will prepare these learners for subsequent hands‑on inspection and maintenance work.
Learning Objectives:• Describe the purpose, construction and operating principles of DC instrument transformers (shunts, DCCTs/Hall sensors) and auxiliary transformers and label major components on a diagram. • Differentiate shunt and DC current transformer behavior and state two inspection indicators for each type. • Identify common installation and wiring defects for DC instrument and auxiliary transformers and match each to its likely cause. • Perform a structured visual inspection using a provided checklist and record all observed defects. • Measure insulation resistance and continuity on transformer windings/secondaries with site test equipment, record readings, and compare to acceptance criteria. • Where applicable, verify transformer polarity/ratio and log results against reference values. • Assess burden and secondary circuit integrity by measuring continuity and voltage drop and documenting measured values. • Conduct basic maintenance tasks (tighten connections, clean contacts, replace minor components) per site procedure and demonstrate completion on one component. • Apply correct isolation and earthing sequences on a mock or diagrammed task and verify compliance with site procedure. • Interpret diagnostic and test data to classify equipment condition as Acceptable / Requires Repair / Unsafe and justify the classification with measured evidence. • Complete a standardized inspection and test report including readings, observations, maintenance actions and recommended follow‑up. • Escalate significant or complex faults by preparing and submitting an incident/escalation report containing required technical details for protection or specialist teams.

202.1How to Read and Interpret Circuit PrintsCourse Title:202.1 How to Read and Interpret Circuit Prints
Course Structure:Module 1: American National Standards Institute (ANSI) & Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers (IEEE)
• Become familiar with ANSI/IEEE nomenclature
Module 2: Local Prints
• Explain and interpret local prints
Course Duration:4 Hours0 Minutes4
Course Description:This course teaches REWs how to read and interpret circuit prints by using standard ANSI/IEEE nomenclature and local SoundTransit/King County Rail drawing conventions. Learners will become familiar with common symbols, abbreviations, and phasing / connection notations from ANSI and IEEE. They will then apply that knowledge to locate components, trace circuits, and interpret protection, control, and power wiring on local prints. Practical exercises focus on translating drawings into on‑site actions, verifying nameplate and terminal information, and identifying discrepancies that require specialist follow‑up.
Course Outcomes:Technicians will be able to recognize ANSI/IEEE symbols and express common ANSI/IEEE nomenclature, while also interpreting local SoundTransit/King County Rail circuit prints, and locating components. They will also be able to trace protection, control, and power wiring; verify nameplate and terminal information against drawings; translate prints into on‑site actions; identify drawing discrepancies; and produce clear notes or escalation reports for supervisor follow‑up.
Learning Objectives:• Identify and name 20 common ANSI/IEEE schematic symbols and abbreviations from a provided symbol chart. • Explain five key ANSI/IEEE nomenclature terms (e.g., phasing, polarity, terminal designation) and give one example of each. • Interpret local SoundTransit/King County Rail drawing conventions and map three local symbols to their ANSI/IEEE equivalents. • Locate specified components (breakers, relays, transformers, disconnects) on a supplied circuit print within five minutes. • Trace and document the complete protection circuit path for a given fault scenario on a provided print. • Trace and document control and power wiring routes between two designated terminals on a sample drawing. • Verify nameplate and terminal information against a circuit print for two pieces of equipment and record any mismatches. • Translate a circuit print into a step‑by‑step on‑site action checklist for isolation or testing tasks. • Detect and describe at least three drawing discrepancies or unclear items on a sample print and classify each as Minor / Needs Clarification / Requires Escalation. • Produce a clear escalation or technician report containing required drawing references, observed discrepancies, and recommended next steps for supervisor review.
