202.2Inspect and Maintain Substation ComponentsCourse Title:202.2 Inspect and Maintain Substation Components - Part 1: Traction Power Substation Maintenance Standard
Part 1: Traction Power Substation Maintenance Standard
Course Structure:Module 1: Traction Power Substation Maintenance Standard
• Review and become familiar with Sound Transit Traction Power Substation Maintenance Standard (Use most recently published version, per calendar date.)
Double-Click to Open Most Recent Version
Course Duration:TBD HourTBD MinutesTBD1
Course Description:This intermediate course is intended to refresh and further instill Sound Transit’s OCS Maintenance Standard by covering its purpose, scope, and applicable locations (Line 1, Line 2, OMF‑C/E). Learners will further understand roles and responsibilities for safe OCS work, required inspection, and functional testing routines. Heightened focus will be placed on preventive inspection frequencies, and key component terminology. The course reinforces and expounds upon the approved Order of Operation for isolation, testing, earthing / grounding, and return‑to‑service; as well as how to map single‑line diagrams to plant. Emphasis is again placed on correct recordkeeping and event logging in EAMS, recognizing priority defect ratings, and following escalation and handover procedures to support standards‑compliant OCS maintenance and asset management.
Course Outcomes:By the end of this course, the intermediate REW learning audience members will be able to explain the purpose, scope and applicable locations of Sound Transit’s OCS Maintenance Standard; describe roles and responsibilities for safe OCS work; perform required inspections and functional tests at the prescribed frequencies; map single‑line diagrams to plant and identify key OCS components; apply the approved Order of Operation for isolation, testing, earthing/grounding and return‑to‑service; record and preserve event logs and test data in EAMS; classify defects using priority ratings; and follow escalation and handover procedures to ensure standards‑compliant OCS maintenance and asset management.
Learning Objectives:• Explain the purpose and objectives of the OCS Maintenance Standard, and list the specific locations where it applies (Line 1, Line 2, OMF‑C/E), including why adherence matters for safety and asset reliability. • Summarize the Standard’s scope and clearly state typical exclusions, giving examples of when alternate documents apply (e.g., Link T procedures, future network extensions) and how to confirm the applicable document. • Identify the intended audience and outline the roles and responsibilities of Sound Transit, King County Metro (KCM) and contractors, including who approves work, who performs inspections, and who manages escalations. • Locate and define key OCS terms and component names used in the Standard, and match each term to its function in the overhead contact system. • Read single‑line diagrams and asset tags, then map diagram items to physical plant by locating at least three named components on site using an SLD and asset tag reference. • Perform basic condition assessments using the FTA 1–5 rating scale, explain Useful Life Benchmarks, and assign a condition rating to sample component photos or inspection data. • Describe required functional test types (e.g., contact geometry, section insulator checks, mechanical operation) and state the minimum inspection and maintenance frequencies at a program level. • Maintain required records: update and store single‑line diagrams and configuration files, and correctly enter inspection and test results into EAMS according to site naming and data conventions. • Log incidents accurately by recording date/time, personnel involved, equipment IDs, suspected causes, immediate actions taken, and create Engineering Service Requests (ESRs) when specialist input is required. • Explain Priority 1–3 defect ratings, list required immediate and follow‑up actions for each priority, and describe return‑to‑service considerations and temporary measures. • Identify qualified person categories (Lead, REW, Superintendent, Chief), state the minimum qualifications/training for each category, and summarize the appointment and competency verification process. • Apply escalation and handover procedures: preserve event logs and test records, report defects per the Standard, and demonstrate when and how to request protection or engineering review using standard forms and communication channels.

Learning Objectives:• Explain the purpose and operating principles of substation transformers and rectifier assemblies and label major components on a diagram. • List five common failure modes for transformers and rectifiers and match each to typical visual or test indicators. • Describe protection and cooling arrangements used on traction substation equipment and state two inspection points for each. • Perform a structured visual inspection using a provided checklist and record all defects and condition observations. • Measure insulation resistance on transformer windings and rectifier assemblies, record readings, and compare them to specified acceptance limits. • Verify transformer ratio and polarity, log measured values, and flag deviations beyond tolerance. • Conduct thermal monitoring (IR/temperature probe) on transformer and rectifier cooling elements, record temperatures, and identify abnormal readings. • Test rectifier diodes/bridges using the prescribed procedure, document pass/fail outcomes, and isolate faulty units for escalation. • Inspect and perform basic maintenance on tap‑changer components per site procedure and demonstrate one adjustment or cleaning task. • Apply correct isolation and earthing sequences on a mock setup and verify compliance with site safety requirements. • Interpret diagnostic and test data to classify equipment condition as Acceptable / Requires Repair / Unsafe and justify the classification with recorded evidence. • Complete standardized inspection and test reports with readings, observations, maintenance actions and recommended follow‑up, and submit escalation reports when specialist input is required.

202.2Inspect and Maintain Substation ComponentsCourse Title:202.2 Inspect and Maintain Substation Components - Part 3: Substation Components - AC & DC Breakers
Part 3: Substation Components - AC & DC Breakers
Course Structure:Module 1: Substation Components: AC Breakers
• Inspect and maintain AC breakers
Module 2: Substation Components: DC Breakers
• Inspect and maintain DC breakers
Course Duration:TBD Hours0 MinutesTBD1
Course Description:This intermediate learning offering teaches REWs how to inspect and maintain AC and DC substation circuit breakers used in traction and depot systems. Technicians in training will study breaker types, operating principles, auxiliary equipment, and common failure modes. The course covers structured visual and mechanical inspections, contact resistance and timing tests, trip‑circuit and secondary wiring checks, and basic maintenance tasks. Emphasis is placed on correct isolation, earthing and safety procedures for both AC and DC systems. Participants learn to interpret test results, document findings, and follow escalation routes for protection or specialist intervention. Practical examples and exercises prepare learners for subsequent hands‑on breaker maintenance workshops.
Course Outcomes:Technicians will identify AC and DC breaker types, auxiliary components, and common failure modes. They will perform structured inspections, measure and interpret contact resistance and timing tests, verify trip‑circuit and secondary wiring integrity, apply correct isolation and grounding procedures, complete accurate test records, and escalate protection or breaker faults to specialists while preparing for hands‑on maintenance workshops.
Learning Objectives:• Identify five common AC and three common DC breaker types and label their major auxiliary components on a diagram. • List six typical failure modes for breakers and match each to its likely visual or test indicator. • Perform a structured visual and mechanical inspection using the provided checklist and record all defects. • Measure contact resistance on a breaker, record milliohm readings, and compare results to acceptance criteria. • Conduct a breaker timing test, record open/close times, and assess results against pass/fail thresholds. • Verify trip‑circuit and secondary wiring continuity and insulation, document test values, and flag anomalies. • Select and apply the correct isolation and earthing sequence for a given AC or DC breaker scenario on a mock setup. • Apply site safety procedures and PPE for both AC and DC breaker work and demonstrate correct lockout/tagout practice. • Interpret inspection and test data to classify equipment condition as Acceptable / Requires Repair / Unsafe with supporting evidence. • Complete a standardized test report including readings, observations, maintenance actions and recommended next steps. • Prepare and submit an escalation report for protection or breaker faults containing required technical details for specialist review. • Demonstrate one basic maintenance task (e.g., contact cleaning, lubrication, fastening) on a breaker per site procedure.

Part 4: Substation Components - Protective Relays

• Inspect and maintain protective relays
Module 2: Substation Components: UPS and Station Battery Banks
• Inspect and maintain Uninterruptible Power Supply (UPS) and station battery banks
Module 3: Substation Components: Auxiliary Relay Contacts
• Inspect HVAC and Lighting
Course Duration:TBD Hours0 MinutesTBD1
Course Description:This intermediate-level course trains REWs to inspect and maintain protective relays, UPS systems and station battery banks, and auxiliary relay contacts that control HVAC and lighting in substations. Learners study relay types, trip logic and common failure modes, and perform relay functional checks and secondary wiring inspections. The module covers UPS operation, battery health assessment, charging systems, and routine battery maintenance. Participants carry out visual inspections, insulation and continuity tests, and record trending data for thermal and voltage anomalies. Emphasis is placed on correct isolation and earthing, safe test procedures, interpreting diagnostic results, and documenting findings. Practical exercises teach fault identification, escalation routes to protection or specialist teams, and preparation for subsequent hands‑on maintenance workshops.
Course Outcomes:By the end of this course, technicians in training will begin performing structured inspections and functional checks on protective relays; start verifying secondary wiring and trip logic; express their understanding of how to assess UPS operation and station battery health; and begin carrying out routine battery maintenance. They will record and trend thermal and voltage data, run insulation and continuity tests, and interpret diagnostic results to determine equipment condition. Learners will apply correct isolation and earthing procedures, follow safe test protocols, document findings and test records accurately, and escalate faults or complex issues to protection or specialist teams while being prepared for hands‑on maintenance workshops.
Learning Objectives:• Identify common protective relay types and explain trip logic for three typical relay functions. • Perform a relay functional test, record results, and verify operation against expected trip settings. • Inspect secondary relay wiring and terminal connections and document any wiring faults. • Measure insulation resistance and continuity on relay secondary circuits and compare readings to acceptance criteria. • Describe three common relay failure modes and match each to likely diagnostic indicators. • Inspect a UPS system, record input/output voltages and frequencies, and flag deviations from normal ranges. • Perform a battery health check (voltage, specific gravity or equivalent, and internal resistance), record values, and classify battery condition. • Verify battery charger operation and log charging current and voltage trends over a defined period. • Conduct visual and thermal inspections on UPS and battery equipment, capture IR readings, and report temperatures outside normal limits. • Test and verify auxiliary relay contacts for HVAC and lighting control, logging continuity and operation results. • Apply correct isolation and earthing sequences on a mock procedure and demonstrate compliance with site safety rules. • Complete standardized inspection and test reports with measured data, observations, and recommended actions, and submit escalation reports for faults requiring specialist review.

203.1Preparing to Work on Overhead Contact SystemCourse Title:203.1 Preparing to Work on Overhead Contact System
Course Structure:Module 1: Overhead Contact System - Work Preparation
• Describe and explain safety procedures for working at heights and fall protection
Module 2: Overhead Contact System - Sectionalization
• Explain sectionalization
Module 3: Overhead Contact System - Overhead Contact Rail
• Describe the overhead contact rail and its function in relation to other OCS components
Module 3: Overhead Contact System - Floating Bridge Expansion Joints
• Discuss floating bridge expansion joints
Module 4: Substation Components: Auxiliary Relay Contacts
• Explain how to prepare for operations on the overhead contact rail
Course Duration:TBD Hours0 MinutesTBD1
Course Description:This intermediate course prepares REWs to safely plan and execute work on the Overhead Contact System. Learners review working‑at‑height procedures, fall‑protection requirements, and site rigging best practices. The module explains sectionalization principles and how to identify and isolate OCS sections for safe access. Participants study the overhead contact rail, its role within the OCS and its interfaces with supports, insulators and feeders. The course covers floating bridge expansion joints and their inspection and handling considerations. Emphasis is placed on pre‑work planning, required permits and equipment, correct PPE and tools, coordination with substation and protection teams, and specific preparatory steps for operations on the overhead contact rail.
Course Outcomes:By the end of this course, technicians will be expected to apply working‑at‑height and fall‑protection procedures, select and use appropriate rigging and PPE, identify and implement sectionalization to isolate OCS segments, and locate and describe overhead contact rail interfaces with supports, insulators and feeders. They will recognize floating bridge expansion joint issues and follow handling/inspection precautions, complete required pre‑work planning and permitting steps, coordinate with substation and protection teams, and prepare the site and equipment for safe overhead contact rail operations.
Learning Objectives:• Demonstrate correct selection and fit of fall‑protection PPE and lanyards for a given OCS work task. • Explain how to perform a pre‑work rigging check and set up fall‑arrest anchors to meet site load and clearance requirements. • Describe sectionalization and identify the isolation points for a specified OCS segment on a single‑line diagram. • Execute a mock sectionalization sequence on a diagrammed scenario and verify isolation with team confirmation. • Locate and label overhead contact rail interfaces with supports, insulators and feeders on provided drawings and photos. • Inspect a length of overhead contact rail and record three potential interface defects using the course checklist. • Identify floating bridge expansion joint components and list two inspection criteria and two handling precautions. • Complete a permit and pre‑work checklist for an overhead contact rail operation, including required notifications to substation/protection teams. • Coordinate a simulated handover with protection/substation staff and document the agreed isolation and return‑to‑service steps. • Prepare an on‑site equipment and tools inventory for an OCS rail operation and confirm availability before work commences. • Recognize conditions that require escalation and submit an incident/escalation report containing date/time, personnel, equipment IDs and suspected cause.

203.2 Overhead Contact System Components Course Title:203.2 Overhead Contact System Components - Part 1: Inspection and Maintenance
Part 1: Inspection and MaintenanceCourse Structure:Module 1: Contact Cable
• Inspect, maintain, and repair the contact cable (applying local parameters)
READ THIS NOTEModule 2: Supporting Structure
• Inspect, maintain, and repair supporting structure
Module 3: Insulation
• Inspect, maintain, and wash insulators and insulation
Module 4: Measure OCS Conductors
• Measure OCS conductors
Course Duration:TBD Hours0 MinutesTBD1
Course Description:This intermediate course teaches REWs how to inspect, maintain and perform basic repairs on overhead contact system components. Learners study contact cable condition criteria and local parameter limits and apply approved techniques for cleaning, tensioning and minor repairs. The module covers inspection and upkeep of supporting structures, including brackets, poles and fastenings. Participants learn insulator inspection, washing methods and insulation maintenance to preserve dielectric performance. Instruction includes safe isolation and earthing procedures required before work on OCS conductors. Trainees practice measuring conductor wear, tension and continuity using site test equipment and record results against acceptance criteria. Emphasis is placed on accurate documentation, defect classification, and escalation to specialist teams when limits or safety concerns are identified.
Course Outcomes:By the end of this course, REWs will explain how to correctly inspect and assess contact cable condition using the local parameter checklist and record five condition measurements; perform approved cleaning, tensioning and one minor repair per trainee to specification; complete structured inspections and maintenance of supporting structures and fastenings using the provided checklist; wash and evaluate insulators and verify dielectric condition with a pass/fail megger reading; apply the correct isolation and earthing sequence from the Order of Operation on a mock task; measure conductor wear, tension and continuity with site test equipment, log readings against acceptance limits, and classify defects as Acceptable / Requires Repair / Unsafe; and submit an escalation report for any safety‑critical or out‑of‑limit findings with required technical details.
Learning Objectives:• Describe how to use the local parameter checklist to inspect a contact cable and record five required condition measurements on the provided log sheet. • Explain and demonstrate approved contact cable cleaning and tensioning techniques to meet specification, then describe the supervised minor repair performed and have the instructor verify compliance. • Complete and explain a structured inspection of a mock supporting structure and fastenings using the provided checklist, and submit a defect log with photos or sketches. • Describe the insulator washing procedure, perform it on the training bench, and record the megger test result as Pass or Fail with the measured value. • Measure conductor wear with calipers, record the value in millimeters, and explain whether it meets acceptance limits. • Measure conductor tension using site tension equipment, record the reading in appropriate units, and explain any out‑of‑limit result. • Test conductor continuity with a multimeter, document the resistance reading in ohms, and classify the outcome as Good / High‑Resistance / Open. • Explain and apply the Order of Operation isolation and earthing sequence on a mock setup, obtain team verification, and record the verification time. • Classify each identified defect as Acceptable / Requires Repair / Unsafe and justify the classification with supporting measurements or photos. • Complete the standardized inspection report template, explain each recorded measurement and observation, and include recommended actions. • Prepare and submit an escalation report for any safety‑critical or out‑of‑limit finding, and include date/time, equipment ID, measured values and recommended immediate actions.

Part 2: Replace Contact CableCourse Structure:Module 1: OCS Rigging
• Perform the functions of OCS rigging
Module 2: Contact Cable
• Replace the contact cable
Course Duration:TBD Hours0 MinutesTBD1
Course Description:This intermediate course trains REWs to perform OCS rigging and replace contact cable safely and to standard. Learners study rigging roles, anchor and pulley setup, load calculations, and inspection of lifting gear. The module covers permitted isolation and earthing steps required before rigging or cable work. Participants practice removing worn contact cable, installing new cable, and setting correct tension to local parameters. Instruction includes splice and termination techniques, mechanical and electrical checks, and immediate defect remediation. Emphasis is placed on safe work positioning, communication and team signaling during lifts, tool choice and PPE, post‑work testing, and accurate documentation to prepare trainees for live maintenance tasks.
Course Outcomes:By the end of this course, REWs will perform OCS rigging tasks including anchor and pulley setup, load calculation and lifting‑gear inspection; complete permitted isolation and earthing before rigging; safely remove and install contact cable, apply splices and terminations, and set tension to local parameters; carry out mechanical and electrical post‑work checks and immediate defect remediation; demonstrate correct team signaling, work positioning, tool use and PPE during lifts; and produce accurate post‑job documentation and test records to support live maintenance handovers.
Learning Objectives:• Describe rigging roles and responsibilities and explain team signaling protocols for OCS lifts. • Explain anchor and pulley selection criteria and calculate safe working loads for a given rigging scenario. • Inspect lifting gear and express acceptance or rejection criteria using the provided checklist. • Describe required isolation and earthing steps and demonstrate completion on a mock permit‑to‑work setup. • Explain splice and termination types and show correct execution of one approved splice on the training rig. • Demonstrate removal of worn contact cable following safe work procedures and record steps taken. • Perform installation of new contact cable, set tension to local parameter values, and record measured tension. • Inspect and verify mechanical connections and electrical continuity after installation and log results against acceptance criteria. • Describe common immediate defect remediation actions and perform one corrective task under instructor supervision. • Explain correct tool selection, PPE requirements and safe work positioning for rigging and cable replacement. • Complete a post‑work test sheet and produce accurate documentation including test readings and defect notes. • Discuss criteria for escalation and prepare a sample handover note for live maintenance teams.

203.2 Overhead Contact System Components Course Title:203.2 Overhead Contact System Components - Part 3: More on Inspection and Maintenance

• Inspect and maintain overhead line feeder cable

• Inspect and maintain hangers

• Inspect and maintain equalizing jumper cable

• Inspect and maintain poles
Module 5: Back Guy
• Inspect and maintain back guy (expound on various types)

Course Description:This intermediate course teaches REWs how to inspect, maintain and perform basic repairs on overhead line feeder cables, hangers, equalizing jumper cables, poles and back guys. Learners study construction, function and typical failure modes for each component and learn applicable local acceptance criteria. The module covers structured visual and mechanical inspections, tension and continuity checks, corrosion and fatigue assessment, and approved minor repair techniques. Participants practice measuring cable tension, replacing hangers and jumper lengths, and assessing pole integrity including rot and foundation checks. The course explains different back guy types, their inspection requirements and corrective options. Emphasis is placed on safe isolation and earthing, correct rigging and PPE, accurate documentation of findings, and escalation of safety‑critical defects to control center, supervisors, chiefs, leads, etc.
Course Outcomes:By the end of this course, REWs will inspect and assess overhead line feeder cables, hangers, equalizing jumper cables, poles and back guys against local acceptance criteria; perform structured visual and mechanical inspections, measure cable tension and continuity, and assess corrosion, fatigue and pole foundation integrity; carry out approved minor repairs such as hanger replacement and jumper reinstatement; apply correct isolation, earthing, rigging and PPE for safe work; accurately document measurements, findings and remedial actions; and escalate safety‑critical defects to the control center, supervisors or specialist teams with required technical details.
Learning Objectives:• Describe construction and function of overhead line feeder cables, hangers, equalizing jumpers, poles and back guys. • Explain common failure modes for each component and list applicable local acceptance criteria. • Perform a structured visual inspection on a sample feeder cable or hanger and record at least five condition observations using the provided checklist. • Measure cable tension on a training rig, record the value in N or kgf, and state whether it falls within acceptance limits. • Test jumper and feeder continuity with a multimeter, log resistance readings, and classify results as Good / High‑Resistance / Open. • Inspect poles for rot, cracking or foundation movement, document three measured indicators, and assign a pass/fail judgement. • Assess corrosion and fatigue on hangers and jumper fittings and describe two corrective options for each defect type. • Replace a hanger or reinstate a jumper on the training rig following procedure and have the instructor verify correct technique. • Explain inspection requirements and corrective measures for at least three back guy types and note when replacement is required. • Apply the correct isolation, earthing and rigging sequence on a mock task and obtain team verification. • Complete a standardized inspection report with measurements, photos and recommended actions and submit it for review. • Prepare and submit an escalation notice for any safety‑critical defect including date/time, equipment ID, measured values and recommended immediate actions.

204.1Preparing to Work on Overhead Catenary System Course Title:204.1 Preparing to Work on Overhead Catenary System
Course Structure:Module 1: Overhead Catenary System - Work Preparation
• Understand and follow safety procedures for working at heights and fall protection
Module 2: Overhead Catenary System - Sectionalization
• Describe sectionalization
Module 3: Overhead Catenary System - Energized / De-Energized
• Explain energized vs. de-energized
Course Duration:1 Hours0 Minutes1
Course Description:This intermediate course prepares REWs to plan and execute safe work on the Overhead Catenary System. Learners review working‑at‑height procedures and fall‑protection requirements and practice selecting and fitting appropriate PPE. The module explains sectionalization principles and how to identify and isolate catenary sections for safe access. Participants learn the differences between energized and de‑energized states and the implications for permits, testing and work methods. Emphasis is placed on correct isolation, earthing, verification procedures, coordination with protection and substation teams, and documenting pre‑work checks and handovers.
Course Outcomes:By the end of this course, REWs will correctly select and fit fall‑protection PPE and demonstrate working‑at‑height procedures. They will explain sectionalization and identify isolation points on single‑line diagrams and in the field. Learners will distinguish energized and de‑energized states and state required permits, tests and safe work methods for each. Participants will apply the approved isolation, earthing and verification sequence on a mock task and obtain team sign‑off. Finally, trainees will coordinate pre‑work checks with protection and substation teams and produce complete handover documentation.
Learning Objectives:• Describe required fall‑protection PPE and demonstrate correct donning and fit during a live fit‑check. • Explain working‑at‑height procedures and perform a mock rescue/recovery drill per site protocol. • Define sectionalization and identify isolation points for a given catenary segment on a provided single‑line diagram. • Locate and mark isolation points in the field for a specified span using the diagram and asset tags. • Explain the differences between energized and de‑energized states and list required permits and tests for each. • Describe verification tests needed to prove de‑energized status and perform them on a mock setup, recording results. • Apply the approved isolation and earthing sequence on a simulated task and obtain team verification/sign‑off. • Demonstrate coordination steps with protection and substation teams by completing a simulated notification and handover checklist. • Complete a pre‑work checklist and produce required handover documentation including permit references and verification timestamps. • Identify three conditions that require escalation and prepare a sample escalation note with date/time, personnel and recommended actions.

204.2Overhead Catenary System: Inspection and MaintenanceCourse Title:204.2 Part 1: Intro to Overhead Catenary System Messenger Wire / Contact Wire
Part 1 Intro to Overhead Catenary System Messenger Wire / Contact Wire
Course Structure:Module 1: Overhead Catenary System - Messenger Wire / Contact Wire
• Measure and install messenger wire, staggering contact wire to prevent wear on pantograph
Module 2: Overhead Catenary System - Hangers
• Inspect and maintain hangers
Module 3: Overhead Catenary System - Overhead Line
• Inspect and maintain overhead line feeder wire
Module 4: Overhead Catenary System - Poles
• Inspect and maintain poles
Course Duration:TBD Hours0 MinutesTBD1
Course Description:This intermediate course introduces REWs to messenger and contact wire systems and related OCS components. Learners measure, install and stagger messenger and contact wires to control pantograph wear. The module covers hanger inspection, maintenance and replacement techniques. Participants inspect and maintain overhead line feeder wire and assess pole condition including foundations and fixtures. Emphasis is placed on correct isolation, earthing and rigging before work, use of measurement and tensioning tools, recording measurements against local limits, and documenting defects and maintenance actions. Practical exercises prepare trainees for live installation and maintenance tasks.
Course Outcomes:By the end of this course, REWs will accurately measure messenger and contact wire dimensions and calculate stagger values to meet pantograph wear limits; verify tension settings against local parameters and record readings. They will complete hanger and overhead feeder inspection checklists, identify defects, and specify required maintenance or replacement actions. Learners will assess pole condition using defined acceptance criteria, document foundation and fixture indicators, and select the correct isolation, earthing and rigging sequence for a given scenario. They will log all measurements and observations in the standard report template and submit escalation notices for any safety‑critical or out‑of‑limit findings with required technical details.
Learning Objectives:• Describe messenger and contact wire types and explain how staggering reduces pantograph wear. • Measure wire dimensions and calculate stagger values from given span data, recording results to the template. • Verify contact and messenger wire tension against local parameters and log measured readings with units. • Explain acceptable tolerance limits for wire dimensions and tension and identify out‑of‑limit conditions. • Complete the hanger inspection checklist for a provided scenario and list any defects with severity classification. • Specify maintenance or replacement actions for identified hanger or feeder wire defects using the site decision guide. • Describe pole condition acceptance criteria and record three foundation or fixture indicators per inspection form. • Select the correct isolation, earthing and rigging sequence for a given work scenario and justify the choice. • Explain required PPE and rigging checks for OCS work and confirm tool and equipment IDs prior to task start. • Record all measurements and observations in the standard report template and produce a clear summary of required follow‑up. • Draft an escalation notice for any safety‑critical or out‑of‑limit finding including date/time, equipment IDs, measured values and recommended immediate action.

204.2Overhead Catenary System: Inspection and MaintenanceCourse Title:204.2 Part 2 Overhead Catenary System - Wire Tension
Part 2 Overhead Catenary System - Wire Tension
Course Structure:Module 1: Overhead Catenary System - Wire Tensioning
• Check and adjust wire tension
• Check and adjust fixed tension wires
• Check and adjust auto (constant) tension
Course Duration:TBD HoursTBD MinutesTBD1
Course Description:This intermediate course teaches REWs how to check and adjust wire tension in overhead catenary systems. Learners will review tension principles and measurement techniques, inspect and adjust fixed‑tension conductors, and operate and verify auto‑tension (constant tension) systems. The module covers required isolation, earthing and rigging before tensioning, safe tool selection and calibration, acceptable tension limits and tolerance checks, and procedures for greasing or servicing auto‑tension mechanisms. Emphasis is placed on recording measured values against acceptance criteria, interpreting results, applying corrective adjustments, and escalating out‑of‑limit or safety‑critical findings for specialist follow‑up. Practical exercises prepare trainees for live tensioning tasks.
Course Outcomes:By the end of this course, REWs will explain wire tension principles and demonstrate use of tension‑measuring tools, inspect and adjust fixed‑tension conductors to specified limits, and operate and verify auto‑tension systems. They will apply required isolation, earthing and rigging steps before tensioning, select and check tools for correct calibration, and compare measured values to acceptance criteria and tolerances. Learners will document readings and adjustments on standard forms, discuss when tension conditions are unsafe or out‑of‑limit, and identify when and how to escalate issues for specialist follow‑up.
Learning Objectives:• Describe wire tension principles and explain how temperature, span length and hardware affect catenary tension. • Explain the purpose and operation of fixed‑tension and auto‑tension (constant tension) systems and discuss where each is used. • Describe required isolation, earthing and rigging steps before tensioning and list the consequences of skipping any step. • Explain how to select and check tension‑measuring tools for correct calibration and record tool ID and date of last calibration. • Measure tension on a sample fixed‑tension conductor, express the result in the correct units, and compare it to acceptance limits. • Adjust a fixed‑tension conductor in a classroom or mock scenario and record before/after readings on the standard form. • Describe how to operate an auto‑tension system and explain how to verify that it is maintaining constant tension within tolerance. • Explain greasing or servicing procedures for auto‑tension mechanisms and list key inspection points for wear or damage. • Record measured values and any adjustments made on a provided tensioning log and verify that all required fields are complete. • Discuss examples of unsafe or out‑of‑limit tension conditions and identify which cases require immediate escalation. • Describe the escalation process for tension‑related defects and complete a sample escalation form with all required technical details.

204.3Overhead Catenary System: Section Insulation (Various)Course Title:204.3 Overhead Catenary System: Section Insulation (Various)
Course Structure:Module 1: Arc Horns and Support Structure
• Check and adjust arc horns
• Check and adjust support structure
Course Duration:TBD HoursTBD MinutesTBD1
Course Description:This intermediate course instructs REWs on inspecting and maintaining section insulation components with a focus on arc horns and their support structures. Learners study arc horn function, placement and acceptable clearances, and practice visual and mechanical checks to detect wear, alignment and damage. The course covers support‑structure inspection and adjustment techniques for brackets, insulators and mountings, plus criteria for secure fixing and movement allowances. Participants learn required isolation, earthing and verification steps before work, correct use of measurement and adjustment tools, and approved minor remediation or temporary mitigation methods. Emphasis is placed on recording measurements and defects, comparing findings to acceptance limits, applying safe temporary measures where needed, and escalating safety‑critical issues with clear documentation. Practical diagram exercises and hands‑on adjustments prepare trainees for field inspection and maintenance tasks.
Course Outcomes:By the end of this course, REWs will accurately describe arc horn function and placement, perform visual and mechanical checks for wear and alignment, and inspect support structures for secure fixing and movement. They will apply correct isolation and earthing procedures, use measurement tools to record data against acceptance limits, and execute approved minor adjustments or temporary measures. Learners will document all findings clearly and escalate safety‑critical issues for further evaluation. Practical exercises will ensure readiness for field inspection and maintenance tasks.
Learning Objectives:• Describe the function and placement of arc horns within the Overhead Catenary System and explain their role in controlling electrical arcing. • Explain acceptable clearance limits for arc horns and discuss the implications of misalignment or wear. • Perform visual and mechanical checks on arc horns using a checklist to identify wear, alignment issues, and damage. • Inspect support structures, including brackets and mountings, and assess secure fixing and movement allowances based on given criteria. • Demonstrate correct isolation and earthing procedures prior to inspection and maintenance tasks. • Use measurement tools to accurately record arc horn and support structure data, comparing results to established acceptance limits. • Execute approved minor adjustments or temporary mitigation methods on arc horns and support structures when required. • Document all measurements, findings, and corrective actions clearly on standard reporting forms. • Identify conditions that require escalation and prepare a report detailing the issue along with recommended further evaluation steps. • Participate in practical diagram exercises to solidify understanding and readiness for real-world field inspection and maintenance tasks.
